summary: Extends the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) so a PCE can compute and set up Segment Routing paths in the IPv6 data plane, adding to existing support for the MPLS data plane.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9603 extends PCEP so a path-computation element can send an IPv6 Segment Routing path to a router. The peers exchange capability information, then carry each path segment in new route subobjects.

questions: what is the srv6 ero subobject
what is path setup type 3 in pcep
subtitle: Extends PCEP so a path-computation element can provide paths for IPv6 Segment Routing.

tldr.problem: PCEP already supported Segment Routing for MPLS, but lacked the objects and procedures to exchange paths for the IPv6 data plane.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Path Setup Type 3, an SRv6 capability sub-TLV, and SRv6-ERO and SRv6-RRO subobjects carrying SIDs and optional node or adjacency identifiers.
tldr.outcome: PCEs can compute or initiate SRv6 paths for PCCs, subject to advertised capabilities and Maximum SID Depth. RFC 9603 has been updated by RFC 9756 and RFC 9933.

today: RFC 9603 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2024. It has been updated by RFC 9756 and RFC 9933.

sections.title: PCEP Paths for the IPv6 Data Plane
sections.content:
Segment Routing steers packets with an ordered list of segments. PCEP allows a Path Computation Client (PCC) and Path Computation Element (PCE) to exchange path information. RFC 8664 defined PCEP support for the MPLS data plane; RFC 9603 extends it to SRv6.

A PCC can request an SRv6 path from a stateful or stateless PCE. A controller acting as a PCE can also instantiate candidate paths on a head-end PCC. In PCEP terminology, an LSP corresponds to an SRv6 path represented by a list of IPv6 SIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEP already carried segment-routing paths for MPLS. This RFC adds the formats and rules needed to carry paths made from IPv6 SIDs.

sections.title: Exchanging SRv6 Capability
sections.content:
Path Setup Type (PST) 3 means that a path uses SRv6. A PCEP peer advertises support in the OPEN exchange and includes the SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV, type 27. A request or stateful request object for an SRv6 path MUST include a PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV with PST set to 3.

The capability can include Maximum SID Depth (MSD) information. The PCE MUST NOT send a path that exceeds the PCC's MSD. It also needs to consider MSD for intermediate nodes along the path, which may be learned from IGP or BGP-LS.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers announce SRv6 support when they open a PCEP session. The request identifies the path type, and the PCE must keep the number of SIDs within the nodes' supported limits.

sections.title: The SRv6 Explicit Route Subobject
sections.content:
An Explicit Route Object (ERO) contains subobjects that describe a path. The new SRv6-ERO subobject, type 40, carries one segment and can include a 128-bit SID, a Node or Adjacency Identifier (NAI), an endpoint behavior and an optional SID Structure.

Flags indicate whether the SID or NAI is absent, whether the structure is present, and whether the PCC should verify the SID. The optional fields MUST appear in the order SID, NAI, SID Structure. A corresponding SRv6-RRO subobject reports the path actually applied by the PCC and uses the same format without the loose-hop flag.
sections.plainLanguage: Each SRv6-ERO subobject describes one path segment and can carry its SID and related details. The PCC reports the path it actually applied using SRv6-RRO subobjects.

sections.title: Describing the SID Structure
sections.content:
The optional SID Structure describes the lengths of the locator block, locator node, function and argument fields in a SID. It contains four one-octet length fields, followed by reserved bits and flags.

The four lengths are measured in bits and MUST total no more than 128. If the total exceeds 128 bits, the receiver treats the SID as invalid and returns a PCErr with Error-Type 10 and Error-value 37. The structure can help a PCE or operator check SIDs against an allocation scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The optional structure records how many bits belong to each part of a SID. Its four lengths must fit within the SID's 128 bits.

sections.title: Checking and Interpreting a Route
sections.content:
A PCC checks that the subobject length, NAI type and presence flags agree. If they do not, the PCC treats the ERO as invalid and reports an error. The RFC assigns separate error values for malformed objects, unsupported NAI types, missing SID and NAI fields, mixed subobject types, and paths that exceed the PCC's MSD.

The subobjects identify segments in order: the first subobject gives the first segment the traffic is directed to, followed by the next and subsequent segments. An SRv6-ERO is valid only when the peer advertised the required SRv6 capability and PST.
sections.plainLanguage: The PCC checks that each route entry has consistent fields and that the peer negotiated SRv6. It then reads subobjects in order to determine the sequence of segments.

sections.title: Session Security and Registrations
sections.content:
A controller can use these extensions to instantiate an SRv6 path. Without integrity protection, an attacker could alter a path and avoid further verification. The MSD value can also reveal a node's forwarding capability. The RFC RECOMMENDS securing PCEP sessions with TLS.

IANA assigned type 40 to the SRv6-ERO and SRv6-RRO subobjects, type 27 to the capability sub-TLV, and PST 3 to SRv6. It also created registries for NAI types and flags.
sections.plainLanguage: Because PCEP can install paths, peers need integrity protection against changed instructions. The RFC recommends TLS and registers identifiers used by the new PCEP fields.
